name: Macau
summary: A Portuguese trading post on the south China coast from 1557, the first and last European colony in China; returned to China in 1999 as a Special Administrative Region, now a world gambling centre.

knownFor.label: Casinos
knownFor.note: Largest gambling centre in the world.

location.value: Southern China, on the Pearl River estuary; land area 32.9 km² (the text; the infobox gives a total of 119.3 km²).

terrain.value: A small peninsula and the former islands of Taipa and Coloane, now joined by the reclaimed Cotai strip.

climate.value: Humid subtropical, with hot, rainy summers, mild winters and typhoons mainly from July to September.

resources.value: A sheltered harbour at the mouth of the Pearl River and its position between China and the sea; almost no natural resources.

disasters.value: Typhoons such as Hato (2017), which flooded much of the city, and storm surges in low-lying areas.

population.value: 712,651 (2024 estimate, infobox); the text gives 667,400 for the end of 2018.

urbanisation.value: Entirely urban, with high-rise housing, casinos on the Cotai strip and the old city centre on the peninsula.

disease.value: Plague and cholera outbreaks struck in the 1800s and early 1900s; modern health care is good.

migration.value: Refugees from mainland China in the 1930s–40s and after 1949, and later migrant workers from the mainland and Southeast Asia.

tradeRoutes.value: Portuguese trade between China, Japan and Europe (1500s–1600s).

wealth.value: GDP per person US$69,430 (2023); HDI 0.934 (2023, infobox).

moneyAndTax.value: The Macanese pataca, issued by the Banco Nacional Ultramarino since 1906; most government income comes from casino taxes.

inequality.value: Large gaps between casino owners and high earners and low-paid service and migrant workers.

governmentType.value: Leased to Portugal by the Ming in 1557; handed over at midnight on 20 December 1999 after 442 years; now a special administrative region under “one country, two systems” with the Basic Law as its constitution.

keyRulers.value: Edmund Ho was the first Chief Executive after 1999; the infobox lists Sam Hou Fai as Chief Executive. Portuguese governors are not covered in the part read.

succession.value: Chosen by a committee and approved by Beijing.

institutions.value: The Basic Law of 1999 sets out “one country, two systems”, with a Chief Executive, a partly elected Legislative Assembly and its own courts.

stability.value: Mostly calm, but the 1-2-3 incident riots of December 1966 weakened Portuguese authority.

eliteConflict.value: Casino owners and pro-Beijing business elites dominate politics; earlier, Portuguese officials depended on Chinese merchants.

armyAndTech.value: Portuguese forts such as the Monte Fortress defended the city; a garrison of China’s People’s Liberation Army has been based there since 1999.

majorWars.value: The Dutch attacked in the 1622 Battle of Macau and were repelled by the Portuguese.

territoryChange.value: Land reclamation more than doubled its area.

alliancesRivals.value: Portugal and China shared power for centuries; rivals included the Dutch and, after 1842, British Hong Kong.

inventions.value: No major inventions; Macau was a channel for European printing, maps and science reaching China.

scienceEducation.value: St Paul’s College (1594), a Jesuit college, was one of the first Western-style colleges in East Asia; the University of Macau dates from 1981.

openness.value: A free port open to many nations; it was the main European gateway to China until Hong Kong grew after 1842.

communicationTransport.value: Ferries, an international airport (1995) and the Hong Kong–Zhuhai–Macau Bridge, opened in 2018.

religion.value: About 80% of the population practises Buddhism and 6.7% follows Christianity; the Catholic share is not given.

languageWriting.value: Chinese (mostly spoken as Cantonese) and Portuguese are both official; the Macanese creole, Patuá, is now nearly extinct.

artsArchitecture.value: The Historic Centre of Macau, with the ruins of St Paul’s and the A-Ma Temple, became a World Heritage Site in 2005.

socialStructure.value: A large Chinese majority, a small Macanese (mixed Portuguese–Asian) community, Portuguese residents and migrant workers.

sharedIdentity.value: A mix of Chinese and Portuguese heritage, seen in food, buildings and festivals, alongside strong local Cantonese culture.

dailyLife.value: Crowded apartment living, work in casinos and tourism, and Macanese dishes such as minchi and Portuguese egg tarts.

neighbours.value: Zhuhai in Guangdong province, mainland China, directly to the north, and Hong Kong about 60 km across the Pearl River estuary.

ideasReligions.value: Jesuit mission base for China and Japan.

colonisation.value: Portugal gained perpetual colonial rights in the 1887 Sino-Portuguese Treaty of Peking.

riseSignals.value: Leased to Portugal by the Ming dynasty as a trading post in 1557.

peakPeriod.value: In the late 16th century Macau was the key link for exporting Chinese silk to Japan; the page gives no dates for the “golden age”.

declineSignals.value: Lost Japan trade (1639); overtaken by Hong Kong.

outcome.value: Handed over to China at midnight on 20 December 1999; now a Special Administrative Region.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
